utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before giving the opportunity to the Defence to continue the examination-in-chief of the witness, I'd like to make sure that everyone understands quite well by now what the speed of speech, since the interpretation had some difficulties yesterday, and apart from that, I would like to indicate to the Prosecution that if it comes to testimony on more specific places within the town of Sarajevo, it might be of great help for the understanding of the Chamber, sometimes they have the, in one way or the other, a map or something available so that we can better follow the testimony. Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed. I see that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is standing up. Is there any remark you'd like to make, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, quite, Mr. President. First of all, I think I've read in the English transcript for the -- that you said Defence. I thought you meant the Prosecution. That's just a minor comment. The Defence, on the other hand, has two points that we would like to raise. First of all, the way in which the hearings are organised, and I don't know whether you would like this to be done in the presence of the witness or not. It is up to you to organise this. Because you said there was a problem in the way in which the hearings were going or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I said we had a problem as far as the translation was concerned and speed of speech, but I do not know whether this is what you refer to or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The problems that the Defence would like to raise at this point are organisational problems for the future with reference to all the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it's a good idea to discusses this at this moment, so I would first like to continue with the examination of Mr. Ashton, and then see whether we can be -- then take a few minutes for you to explain what kind of organisational problems the Defence has and then decide on whether this should be dealt with in closed session or that it could be done in open session. I would suggest to you that we take the last ten minutes of this morning for you to explain what these problems are and not to wait too long to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll be glad to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I indicate already at this moment, because I'm keeping a close eye on the clock, that yesterday the examination-in-chief took two hours and 20 minutes. This is both for your planning and for the Defence planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. In the issue of planning, Your Honours, I was wondering what time do you anticipate taking a break, the first break of the morning so that I can perhaps try to pace the work accordingly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have a morning and an afternoon session, it's intended to have a break at 11.00 for half an hour and then continue the morning session without any other break and then have a lunch break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Blaxill: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ashton. I trust you've rested well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fairly well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did hear His Honour make reference to the speed at which we speak, and I think that's a good word of caution to both of us, because we're dealing in our own native language and that can cause problems to those interpreting. Mr. Ashton, we ended yesterday with my asking you certain questions based on your experiences of different types of projectile, mortar shells and artillery. I have but one further question there, and that is: Were there any particular distinctive sounds or other features that would help one identify fire from a tank as opposed to any other kind of gun?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were distinctive sounds. First of all visual contact with the tank and watching it fire you could quickly determine how the sound of the shell would come forth. The same with artillery. You could hear an artillery piece fire and the shell would come forth in a matter of seconds and you would hear whistling sound that would be followed by the impact, of course. The way the shell would come in and hit something, it would come in at an angle whereas a mortar round would come straight down and leave a star pattern in the street or in a building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any difference in sound of the actual shell from a tank as opposed to an artillery piece?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because tanks were generally fired at close range at objects that I saw in Bosnia in this particular conflict, so the rounds were very rapid from the time of propulsion of the shell out of the barrel to the point of impact was only a matter of seconds. So you didn't hear much of a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you slow down just a little, please, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't hear much of a sound of the shell moving forward, propelling forward until impact. Quite the contrary to artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ashton, I'd like to move to another topic. During the period, let me say, of the winter of 1992 and into the spring of 1993, did you see any incidents of the defensive forces firing out of the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on one occasion I did see the BiH set up a mortar on a position in Sarajevo and fire out three consecutive rounds, and they folded the mortar up and left the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you say firstly: How did you know that the people that you saw were ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Readily identifiable and they were right in the centre of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they identifiable?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had uniforms on and one of them I recognised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the location, where was it that they set up the mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly behind the, at that time, the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe sometime around October of 1992. I'm that not positive. I can't remember that date very well, but it was in 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was staying in the hospital, so it was the latter part of 1992 or early part of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to identify the type or calibre of the mortar they fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an 82-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they left, you say they then left that scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They packed it up and carried it off by hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if that action of firing those rounds drew any fire from other sources onto that spot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative. There was no return fire immediately. Later in the day there was the normal sporadic shelling of the city but not in that area where that incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you say that is the one incident that you saw, did you discover in any other way whether there was any other such fire from the city? In other words, did you hear anything as opposed to see it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on one other occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also in October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall where you heard that noise?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very clearly. I was in the PTT, in UNHCR's office, and I heard a very loud bang of a mortar shell being fired out, and the sound is very distinctive of an outgoing mortar when you're right underneath it. And I learned from the French officers in the PTT, in UNPROFOR, that the BiH had set a mortar up about 70 metres outside of the UNPROFOR headquarters, next to the Egyptian battalion headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other experiences of hearing or seeing outgoing fire from the city --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- during that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have indicated that you travelled around the city quite a lot. Did you see any other kinds of weapons, tanks, mortars, artillery of the ABiH while you were travelling around Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw and where, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ABiH had two tanks that I knew of. One was parked in the tunnel at Ciglane, which I was told could fire a weapon but they didn't have ammunition for it. The other was a tank which I had seen down near the PTT. Then there was an armoured personnel carrier with a heavy machine-gun on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see these particular pieces of ordnance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict they were there. There was another tank which was disabled in an action along the airport road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you at any time see these, for want of a better word, vehicles engaged in any combat operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Noting your earlier comment, Mr. President, while I was proposing to introduce a map, and there are elements on that map which form part of the testimony, I would be quite happy to introduce it now and I think it might be of additional assistance to Your Honours at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It has been served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, this map is precisely one of the problems that we would have liked to look into this morning. The Defence disputes the possibility of including this map in the discussions today since it could have been done earlier. If they wish to do so later, they can do so later, but it will have to go into the minutes that at the present moment, the Defence does not wish to accept this map and the enclosed documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we could answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Blaxill. I still do not know exactly what are the objections against the map. As far as I understand, the map is only meant to give as a better idea about locations and not on any specific -- if there's any specific, you say, this building is not -- or there's no building on that spot, of course we can discuss it, but it's just to have a better geographical idea of what the witness is talking about. So I don't know what exactly your problems are with the map proposed by the Prosecution, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I give you just one element of possible answer, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, last night, quite late, by the way, I poured over this map and I found out that there are handwritten annotations here, as well as a signature of the witness. The handwritten annotations refer to a certain number of types of weapons, which at the time, at the relevant time, would have been covered by certain definitions such as M57, M75, and so on. These elements of information are the points that we should have been able to discuss with General Galic. Let me remind you that your Tribunal has asked for all documentation to be communicated at least seven days prior to the hearing, and we only received all this last night at 1800 hours. As a consequence, we do have data on this map that we are unable to look into today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving an opportunity to Mr. Blaxill to respond, would it be a solution if we use one of the maps that has been used before, put it on the ELMO. It has been marked, I think, already for identification. That's the coloured map without any annotations, and so that we can put it on the ELMO and see whether the witness can find out exactly what spot he means when -- would that be agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, Your Honours, we were going to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: For these purposes, why don't we use a map that is not so contentious. The present map I would correct my learned friend, it was the translation of the annotations that was given to him yesterday, and we can use this later at the appropriate point in the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take a map which is as neutral as possible for this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If we may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Court for intervening in this way. This would have been one of the suggestions from the Defence, that for all witnesses that need to use the map, we should always use the same sort of neutral map so that we can make progress in a neutral fashion and not deviate from it in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- nodding yes, and that's your answer as well. Okay, then You may proceed, Mr. Blaxill, in the way we just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just wondering whether the small coloured map would be suitable, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other neutral map which is helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I think the large black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, the large black and white.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the number off the cuff. Would you indulge me for just a moment, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can sort it out later. We have the neutral black and white, and it's the first one, without any markings on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, P3644 available here, map of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, if that may be placed on the -- given to the witness, we'll have to try and manoeuvre it on the ELMO for any marking if he's going to mark a copy. I would just like to clarify that that is a copy that the witness could mark on? We're not using the original, neutral map. Obviously I don't want him to do that. We have an additional copy, so rather than ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want the witness to mark on the map or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I was thinking principally, if it would assist Your Honours if we go through a number of locations, he could just mark them so we would know or you would know for future reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course I leave it up to you, but for us the most important thing is that we understand the testimony and I want to avoid that we have 150 maps at the end with markings of every single witness, because that would not be very practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If Your Honours are content simply for him to point to places on the map, then I'm quite content to proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, I must apologise, prefers markings on the map. And we have the procedure your colour is, I think, red.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I recall we were red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're using red and if the Defence wants any additional markings before the map will be tendered into evidence in black, or was it in blue? I have to look at that. Yes. So we now have a copy in front of us which is identical to the neutral black and white map, and the original is now returned to the Registry. Is that the original that has been marked for identification? Yes. Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, may I just run through certain places that you have been referring to in your testimony. If you could look at the map and then just indicate. And what I suggest we do, if that suits Their Honours, is we'll just go through numerically 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and that will then be easily cross-referenced to the transcript. Firstly, you stated that you stayed in the State Hospital. Can you give an indication on the map where State Hospital is in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map is of rather poor quality here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just put a little circle with a "1" in it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid any misunderstanding, as far as I see, the top of the map on the ELMO is not the top of the map as it is on paper. Could you please try to turn the map in such a way that the top of the map is also on the top of the ELMO. Otherwise I lose orientation. I think that's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How is that? Can you see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can follow. You're almost in the centre part of the map. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ashton. Would you please first mark State Hospital with the number "1."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right here in Kovaci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you indicate where the Holiday Inn is located that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've marked that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark in relation to that where you say you saw the elderly lady and the young woman, the elderly lady who was shot. If you can perhaps put an "A" near that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly behind the Holiday Inn, directly behind number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could we call that "2A." Number 3, if you would, please, could you indicate where the Presidency building was.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right in this area here. This map is a little bit difficult, because of the grey shades are -- there's a blur here on this map. I don't know if it's on the other copies or not, but it's right in this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just mark that number 3, please. That's fine. Could you mark with the number "4" the location of the PTT building you referred to.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark with the number "5" the approximate location of where you say you saw the mortar being fired by ABiH troops.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That position is exactly number 2, behind number 2, so that would be --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So that will also be position 2?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. 2 is the Holiday Inn. Correction. Number 1, the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 1?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1 is the position where the mortar was in the back of the hospital on the north side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you indicate, please, the location you referred to as Ciglane, and in particular, the tunnel. If you will mark that one, please, number "5." Just hold a second. We --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Number 5 is marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you indicate the location of the incident you recounted when you had the man who was wounded and spoke to you in the street. You will recall from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mark that number "6."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's right in this intersection here, 6 here, just about to the east of the word "Novo Grad" on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also yesterday made reference to a specific incident and container barricades that were there. Can you indicate where those barricades were? I think this is near the Energoinvest?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They are directly across that intersection. From east to west the containers were laid out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you at this stage indicate any other particular intersection or place that you recall there being these sniper barricades?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll just mark onwards, if you would, 7, 8, 9, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just down the street from that is number 7, where the bend in the street is. At the base of Alipasino Polje, by the Presidency, number 8, on Marsala Tita. And across from the Holiday Inn at each of the intersections between the museum and the university, 9, 10. Here would be 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when do you recall those barricades being in place? Were they there throughout your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were put in place while I was in Germany being treated. I came back in September and some of the barricades were there and later on more were put in position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that map, could you also indicate the area of the Jewish cemetery that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I continue with 12?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. And can you just indicate perhaps at this stage broadly with your finger the area you've referred to as Grbavica? And perhaps you can kind of draw just a general circle and we'll put a "G" in there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I outline Grbavica, the front line area that I was familiar with?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was going to ask you that next. So firstly, if you'd just indicate what is the area roughly of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right here there's a big "G."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you recall, let us say the early part of 1993, could you mark in any areas that you recall having seen as front lines between the forces.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just put a little series of "Xs" to indicate the lines you observed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is approximate on this side, because I had never been to that particular front line on the right, on the east side of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have also made reference in your testimony to a place called Vrace, I think it is, or Vrace. Could you indicate, please, where that is, and we'll make that, I think -- are we up to number 13, I think?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vrace is up here on the hill above Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps we can just annotate number, whichever it is now, 14, I think. Could you state -- or indicate, I'm sorry, where the memorial building is you've referred to, the Partizan memorial?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's where I've just put the "14." There's a little park there and a monument.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And you've made reference to having seen a tank belonging to the VRS in that area that came forward and fired. Can you indicate the spot, roughly, where you saw that tank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same position, number 14, next to the monument. There was a flat area there. The tank would roll out onto that area, aim into the city, fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just put a little "T" next to the 14 that would indicate that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it would roll back behind a tree line, a low tree line that was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also indicate where you witnessed -- you referred to any of the armoured vehicles of the ABiH, near the PTT and elsewhere. Can you indicate where you saw those?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Bosnian army; correct, ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the television centre. I'll mark this "15."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that? That was a tank or an APC?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an APC. It was painted blue as a police vehicle. It was not painted green as an army vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've made reference to one or two other positions, in particular one on the lower side of Trebevic Mountain, near the cable car. On that map are you able to give an indication as to where that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I saw there was a Serb tank and Serb artillery, Serb light artillery. Is that what you're indicating?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the site. If you would, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to mark "16" where I saw a tank. It was in this area here. It's hard for me to identify on this map. Again, I make -- this is not clear for me to see here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you feel that it would be in any way inaccurate or misleading, Mr. Ashton, please don't mark that map at this time. I will present another one to you shortly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd prefer to have the larger map so I can see more clearly these ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much. I wonder, a little unconventional perhaps, but do Your Honours at this stage have any other place you recall being mentioned by the witness that you would like marked, we could get it dealt with straight away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Blaxill. I would like to have marked the place where the incident in which the witness was shot on his leg be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may not be on this map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's on the map, you can't mark it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it is. Excuse me, but my memory of that particular incident after it happened sort of was fuzzy. It's in this general area I'm about to mark. It's in one of the streets in this particular area that I'm about to mark right now. Should I put a mark there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it is number 17.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very close to that rail line, because that's where the snipers were sitting, on top of that rail line. Actually, there's a little bend. I don't know if you can see it on your map - right here next to the underpass. That's where it happened, on that bend. So I'm going to take an arrow from the 17 right to that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. I think that concludes for the moment any marking of that particular map. Mr. Ashton, you've already told the Court that in March of 1993 you set up your medical relief agency by the acronym EMRA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did your work in that non-governmental organisation, EMRA, cause you to travel more widely than just the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can give a brief explanation. I was approached by a UNHCR staff member who had done assessment on the Serb side, and she reported to me that the Serbs had critical needs and medicines, and I agreed to go over. The only other organisations working on the Serb side. Can I have the transcript here? Okay. Thank you. The only other agencies working on the Serb side were the International Committee for the Red Cross and Medecins Sans Frontieres. So I went to the Serb side with UNHCR to visit Lukavica barracks, to make my introduction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, firstly: When you refer to the Serb side and Lukavica barracks, who or what was at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there was Major Brane and Major Indic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these -- what was the role of these people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, to my knowledge, as I was introduced to them, were the UN liaison for the United Nations and to the UNPROFOR for the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these people, to your knowledge and observation, serving military people or ...

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult for me to understand Major Indic's position, because I was first introduced to him as Zlatko Mladic's right-hand man for the region, and he had told me that he was his aid and he was with him on most -- in his first introduction he told me a little bit about himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you after that have more dealings with this man and establish his identity more accurately?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, we built a rapport, almost a friendship, and I went on several occasions, two or three times a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you perceive whether he was a serving soldier or had some other role?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, he was a serving soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he -- what sort of clothing did he wear when he was having meetings with yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He usually wore a plain green uniform, sometimes he had a Republika Srpska logo, but generally he was always in a plain green uniform, very neatly pressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain within the overall army in which he served what division or corps or other formation he was actually serving with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a small Romanija Corps flag in his office, and he had, of course, the Republika Srpska flag in there in the office as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you establish in conversation with him or through other direct means whether he was indeed Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as an officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed that particular issue, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards -- you said he had his office in Lukavica barracks. Were you aware of who else, if anyone, had offices in the same -- say, the same building as him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that Major Brane, when he had been transferred out of the PTT building in Sarajevo, after the incident in which the -- I think it was the Bosnian vice-president or vice-premier was shot in the APC coming from the airport. He was moved out of the PTT and over to Lukavica. So he was in that office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you establish whether there were any other officers in that building and to what corps or division they belonged?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw other officers, and I knew there was a barracks there. There were things explained to me in conversation, in general conversation, but not in specific detail, because I didn't ask specific questions, that indicated that it was a military headquarters because there was constant flow of heavy equipment coming in the gate, large lorries, military hardware, tanks, artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to as ascertain whose headquarters Lukavica barracks was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And saying that, army of Republika Srpska, can you state whether there was any division or corps that had its headquarters at that location, specific ones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the markings on the vehicles and only from the markings of some of the people that were there, I assumed it was Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the location of the commander of that corps at the beginning of 1993, say?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never knew where his office was. I encountered him early in 1993, when he was leaving Indic's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you encountered him. Who are you talking about, whom you encountered?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've referred to General Galic. How were you aware that General Galic was the commander of that corps?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was introduced by Major Indic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Did you exchange any conversation with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have any conversation. Indic spoke to him in Serb, and he said to me that -- he explained that I was just there on a humanitarian mission and there was no -- we didn't have any interaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just look to the screen, Mr. Ashton, and slow down a little. I think we're causing a little stress here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you encounter General Galic on any other occasions? Sorry. Do you recall when precisely this encounter with General Galic took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was early 1993. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you encounter General Galic on any other occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him there at Lukavica on two other occasions when I came in early in the morning once, I remember. Also once at a factory up in Pale, were there were several military people. He was there. But I didn't -- I wasn't in proximity to speak to him. I went to see the Minister of Health at the time, and Dr. Starevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in order to -- sorry. In order to pursue the aims of your organisation, you had dealings with, you said, Major Indic. Was that your main contact person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the person I was told I had to go through to do anything. If I travelled on the Serb side, I always notified him. If I planned to leave the city of Sarajevo through Serb territory, I would notify him and he would grant permission at the checkpoints for me to pass through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as a result, were your meetings with him more or less frequent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: More frequent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give an indication on average how often?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally two to three times a week when I was in the area of Sarajevo. There were periods when I was working in other areas of Bosnia that I would only see him once, maybe twice a month, or when I was in Germany, of course, I was out of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you developed a rapport with Major Indic. Did you ever discuss matters pertaining to the conflict and the actions in and around Sarajevo with him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a few occasions I tried to be very careful because I didn't want to make him think that I was doing any kind of intelligence work or doing something that was out of the ordinary, because I was there strictly on a humanitarian mission. But I asked him a few questions about certain events, and when I saw some events which I didn't comment to him about, but -- that were of interest to me, that indicated his authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever mention to him the fact that there were apparently a number of Serb people still within Sarajevo? And what was his response regarding that, if any?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, we had a discussion about Serbs on more than one occasion, living in Sarajevo, who didn't get out, and Indic had sort of a dual opinion of that. The first comments he made to me, the very first comment I remember him making is they had a chance to leave and they chose to stay. He indicated --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He indicated to me at that time that the Serbs were well warned in advance that this was going to happen, but some people chose not to believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the opposing force, as it were, or indeed the population, the Muslim population of Sarajevo? Did he make any comment in respect of his or his compatriots' attitude to him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a certain respect for individuals, especially those who were his teachers in the military, but at the same time he had a very negative attitude about what I call the Bosnians, and he would correct me and call them Muslims and used the term "fanatics."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain whether his was a purely personal opinion or did it reflect any kind of, let us say, political philosophy that might have been doing the rounds at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the communications I had with other Serbs in the territory, it was a general opinion. That's not to say that all Serbs felt that way. Many Serbs had indicated to me that they were very angry about this conflict. They did not want any part of it, and they were forced into the situation. But for the most part, the soldiers that I met, they had the same attitude as Indic, that this was a move to create a fundamentalist Muslim state, was their attitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you've just said, presumably they were against such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and there were many Serbs I encountered who actually classified all Muslims as the same. They took no distinction between combatants or non-combatants or anybody's political philosophy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must state, though --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just watch the speed again, please, Mr. Ashton. I think we're perhaps a little fast.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must state, though, that the longer I was in the former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia, Croatia theatre, I discovered that many people had that attitude on all sides, and it grew among the Bosnians as the war continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you early on or at a certain point in your relationship with Major Indic have any conversation with him about the action involving the city of Sarajevo and maybe what they hoped to achieve by this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He made a comment to me once that he didn't want to destroy the city. He wanted to wear the people down until they would surrender or give up. That's not the exact quote, but that's the exact sentiment of the quote. He also indicated at one point that they could go back to Turkey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said just now about "he," you know, could destroy the city. Did he use the expression so personally or did he refer to --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he used the expression personally. He said "we," collectively, meaning I assume the Serb army or the Serb people or whatever the case may be, could destroy the city if we wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever mention your connection with the State Hospital with him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions. I basically filled Major Indic in on everything I was doing in Bosnia, including on the Bosnian side, and I told him about the conditions at the State Hospital at one point, about shelling of the State Hospital. He indicated to me that that is our hospital, meaning the former JNA hospital, was the military hospital, and he said we wouldn't destroy what we want to take. That's not the exact quote, but it's similar to that particular comment. But he did make the comment that they wanted to get it back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did he respond specifically to the site of the actual damage that you showed him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought him a picture one day and showed him the destruction, and he said, "What a pity." He said, "We obviously can't use it any more." It was generally in that ... Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he mention anything about the shelling of that hospital? I mean, he clearly refers to reaction to the damage, but did he mention anything about the continuation of shelling or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me -- at one time I said to him that I was in the hospital when it was shelled, and he said, "You shouldn't be there when we're shelling it." And he indicated to me, "I have no way to warn you when we're going to shell the city or what targets we're going to shell." And he said, "I would prefer you move to a safer location."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indicate there would be a point at which shelling of the State Hospital would cease?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the Muslims surrendered the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the words, or as accurately as you can recall, the words that he used, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm at a loss for the comment. I know the quote that he used, but I can't think of the exact words at the moment. I actually notated that in one of my journals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage, would it assist you if you were to refer to your journal and check for that to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like the opportunity to refer the journal to Mr. Ashton to assist with his memory. I will ask the appropriate questions about issues as to how contemporaneous and accurate the journal would be for this purpose. I can indicate also that it has been served on my learned friends for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comment on the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are we talking about the personal journal of Mr. Ashton?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, his personal correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In that case, the Defence would like for that document to be produced in its entirety and not just a part of it, as seems to be the case at the moment. Thank you very much in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, certainly I would be proposing to give to Mr. Ashton his documents that formed, as I understand from him, his journal, a mixture of correspondence and personal notes, and indeed in its entirety to him. We do not propose to tender it simply to allow the witness to use it to refresh his memory. That is the sole purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it will not be tendered into evidence, just in order to refresh the memory of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Blaxill, it's not in that particular journal that you have. It was on my computer from Sarajevo. I don't have -- that comment is not in that particular journal that was -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this mean that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have other notes that I took in Bosnia which have not been given to the Tribunal. My comments, though, have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, does this mean that you are not going to use the journal for the purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No. The point has now become academic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps at some point if you do recall the words more precisely, Mr. Ashton, we could perhaps return to that point. So at that time, in 1993, where in fact were you living? Did you move from the State Hospital to another location in town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Around April I moved to Ciglane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout 1993 you performed the duties for the relief organisation, the agency EMRA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall later on in that year, during your meetings with Major Indic, do you recall any occasions when he received communications from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions when I was sitting in the office because he would invite me to come for coffee and sit the morning with him. He rarely tried to discuss military information with me, but we would have general conversations. The phone would ring and he would answer and it would be UNPROFOR, and either his assistant who was there, she would answer the phone and hand it to him or he would answer the phone himself, because he had a direct link to the PTT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that the caller would be from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was on the PTT telephone that their cable that they had put in and he spoke in English to the caller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That leads me to one another question, actually. What about your conversations with Major Indic? Did you use the English language or use an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Major Indic is quite fluent and eloquent in English, very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was the language you used for your transactions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had translators with me at all times, but very rarely did I use them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you therefore, please, indicate certain of these occasions as to what you were able to glean of the message from all the representation from UNPROFOR and what responses you observed on the part of Major Indic and give us an approximate date, if you can.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one occasion in the early -- late spring/early summer of 1993, I believe, when the phone rang -- no. It was earlier than that. It was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: More like in the late winter/early spring. General Morillon called and respectively addressed him. There had been a shelling incident in Marin Dvor in which a child had been killed, and the shelling was continuing, and Morillon asked him, apparently, to order his forces to cease fire. Indic said he was sorry to hear about the incident and he would do his best to look into the matter. And he put the phone down and continued his conversation with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And two questions there. How long did he just continue conversing with you after the telephone call?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please state for the information of the Chamber who was General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the UNPROFOR commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he based?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your subsequent conversation --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Correction. It was General MacKenzie who called at that point. Morillon had had an argument that I had heard earlier. That was a different context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're talking about General MacKenzie. Who was General Mackenzie?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: General MacKenzie at that time had taken Morillon's place as commander for the UNPROFOR. Morillon was force commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember anything of the specific response that Major Indic gave to General Mackenzie?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than he would look into the matter. There was another engagement which I heard, but I don't -- I'm trying to recall the exact comments that were made that day when this particular call we're referring to earlier was made. It carried on for a few moments, and right after that I'd said ten minutes later a call came on another phone in which he spoke Serb. He got into sort of a heated debate with someone, hung that phone up, and continued our conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Major Indic refer on that or any other occasion to any persons to whom he should refer onwards?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said he would pass it on to higher authorities at one time, one conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear him -- you say one conversation. Have you heard any other conversation, maybe not so direct, but as indicating that there was such a relationship to a higher authority for him to do his duties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate some other occasions you've heard words from him to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a couple of incidents in which when I spoke to him he said that he had to -- he had no control over the situation. The situation was in the hand of the higher powers of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he ever specifically identify the higher powers or just refer generically to a chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generically to a chain of command. I never heard him mention the name of anyone that he was going to contact. But there was an incident in which he got on the phone and my translator was sitting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you -- number one, we've been asked to slow down again a little, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, can you say when this was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this was also in mid-1993. Andrej Djordjevic was my translator, a Bosnian Serb who accompanied me to Indic's headquarters. And Indic had gotten on the phone and ordered a ceasefire or for a battery to stop firing while we were in his presence, at which point he asked Biljana, his assistant, to escort us to the reception room at the end of the hallway, and then we continued to hear a very heated argument between him and another commander, according to Andrej, who could hear the conversation through the walls. But I never asked what the conversation was about. It was not my concern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you give us a rough idea, during, let's say, the course of 1993 - it's quite a long period - of how many times you witnessed these kind of conversations whether Indic received some request to stop a certain course of action?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard at least six calls while I was in that office referring to incidents. I actually saw two visits from officers. One was Morillon, when he came over, and that's what I confused the first incident with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall when General Morillon --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was very early in January, when I first -- was first building my relationship with Indic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: January, you say. January 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: January 1993, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last meeting that you ever had with Indic? I mean, how long did you have this relationship with him, working?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the last time I saw Indic was September of 1995. It was right after the NATO bomb, because I went over to visit him to ask him if he was okay, and he made a comment to the effect, "Call your boys off."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that you yourself mentioned some specific incidents to Major Indic when you would meet him. Can you give us an idea of the kind of incidents that you would mention when you did so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I talked to him about the hospital, more specifically. I did refer to other incidents, and I can't recall at the moment what those conversations were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever make reference to civilian casualties --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- as an issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did make reference to civilian casualties and he said that they were just in the way, not in those particular words, but he said in the way -- they were where they shouldn't be or they could have prevented this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was going to say, can you recall now any specific remarks that you can ascribe to his responses to such issues?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. At one point he said, "They can surrender. They can give up."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he make that remark? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was late 1993. I went over there and complained about an incident where a child was killed and he just didn't seem to be concerned about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you had that incident regarding the child, can you recall the words used, or as close as you can recall the words used to express ...

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall if that's the one of the times when he made a derogatory remark about Muslims, but I just can't recall off the top of my head. Again, that's something I have in my personal notes when I kept my personal journals. I did write those comments down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we referring to the journal that is -- or the part of the journal that is in the possession of our office or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative, because these journals -- excuse me. Negative, because these journals were written until early 1993, and then I just kept notes and notebooks. I didn't write full journals about events of the day. I wrote bullet notes about particular comments made to me by people and particular and needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall, for instance, I mean, what did you actually say to him when you mentioned about the incident with the child being killed? Can you recall roughly the words you used?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about -- do you recall anything of your tone when you -- your mood when you were giving -- you know, having that conversation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was quite urgent. I was quite abrupt with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you explain particularly the nature of the incident? What had happened to that child that caused you to raise the issue with Indic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a witness to the event when the shell landed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that that the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was late 1993, but it was down near the barricades, near the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what had been the result of that -- obviously something to do with a child, but what was the actual result of that shell in terms of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one woman wounded, and this child, of course, was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- do you recall the age of the child?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was about 7 years old. It was a male, 7, 8 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that was down near the barricades near the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Right in front of the museum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what else was in the vicinity of the museum? Specifically, was there anything of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were French -- I'm sorry. Translation. There were French and Ukranian forces in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those forces, did they have any vehicles with them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had APCs, and that's the only military hardware they had, but they were stationed three abreast, one at each intersection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those vehicles, what colour were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: White.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they bear markings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN. Clearly marked UN, in black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the soldiers themselves wearing anything distinctive on their heads?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing blue helmets. Some Ukrainians were wearing blue berets at that time. It was actually a quiet time when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any more military people in the area who were not wearing blue helmets or berets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no other military people in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the other people around in that area at the time in civilian clothing or other forms of dress?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were other people around. Quite a few people were travelling on the street that day by foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say what the people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just -- I mean, there were kids with blue jeans and shirts, just normal clothes. There was no -- nothing to indicate any kind of a uniform or anything. Women with dresses. It was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So thinking back now to that incident, can you think again of your meeting with Indic and what may have passed between you by way of the words used?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember -- I don't know if that was that particular incident or it was another incident where he told me that basically -- and I don't -- this is not a direct quote, but he basically said that the Bosnians were worthless and they had no business being there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No business being where?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo. And of course, he referred to it as "the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have also made reference, in fact, to a "derogatory" remark that you recalled regarding Muslims. Can you -- Is it part of this context or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse me just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with the nature of your complaint to Indic for this particular occasion, I mean did you make the allegation that it was the forces of the Bosnian Serbs, the SRK, who had fired it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did indeed, and he didn't deny it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what he said in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said civilians are not -- his exact comment, I'm trying to think of what it was he made. He made a statement about, "We don't determine where the shells go. The shells don't make their choices," or something of that sort. He was referring to the fact that civilians are a casualty of war. But it was specifically about the word "civilians." He did make it clear that civilians are a casualty of -- the result of this action. That I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was stated to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occasion and one other occasion, but I can't recall the other occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us at least an indication of when that might have been?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was earlier in 1993, back in the March area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've referred to there being civilian persons and UNPROFOR troops present. Did you mention to Major Indic that there appeared to be no other military hardware or target in that region when that shell landed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and the way I approached him with that question - and I'm very clear now on that - I said, "Why do you allow this to happen when no one's provoking any problem?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you mean by allowing "this to happen"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allowing a civilian centre to be -- a civilian area to be shelled. Because repeatedly at that particular area there were sniping incidents constantly throughout the war. There were periods of a lull, maybe two, three, sometimes even four weeks, nothing would happen there, and then suddenly there would be sniping and it would go on for two or three weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention that particular aspect to Major Indic --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about the lulls and the change -- I'm sorry. Not about the lulls and the changes in the level of fighting, sniping, and shelling. I never really talked about the causes or the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one point. I'm mindful that the break is coming up very shortly. There's just one issue I'd like to mention, perhaps a little aside from the immediate context. Was there ever an occasion that you raised with Major Indic something that you had first heard about while you were in Germany, something to do with artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Back in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Because my learned friend has just taken a look at the clock more accurately than I have. We are very close, and it would run beyond the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: This would make a more convenient place to break, I think, if that suits Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, once the witness has been brought in, you may proceed in examining him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any reason why the witness is not at hand so that he can be brought to the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, Your Honour. He should be in the waiting room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know. It's only ten metres, so I'm a bit surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, you may resume your exam.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, I raised with you just before the break something to do with something that you discovered or was said to you while you were in Germany, at Rhein-Main air force base. Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a conversation with the Serb logistics liaison officer who was stationed at the air force base there, and we went out one evening, talked a little bit about the situation. He asked me to help him get to America and get out of the situation he was in, and then, in further conversation, he told me in the beginning he was a combatant but associated with Indic and Brane, good friends. And in that conversation he brought up a subject which was totally out of context with the conversation of the shelling of Sarajevo when I brought up some of the incidents that I had seen. I specifically mentioned one incident in which the area around the PTT was heavily shelled and the shells came down the street and I had a photo sequence of this event, and I showed him the photos that I had with me. And he said, "Oh, yes. This is the iron cross."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he explain what the iron cross was meant to be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. He explained to me that the iron cross was a form of punishment which was used whenever a Serb was killed on the other side by Bosnian fire or if the Bosnians fired a mortar round, the Serbs would respond with a very heavy, intense shelling in the pattern of what he called the orthodox cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever mention that particular term to Major Indic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because I found it kind of an odd expression and an odd way of fighting a war. And when I came back into Republika Srpska and met with Indic in one conversation I asked him outright about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that conversation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was early 1993, I believe. It could have been late 1992, because I was at the Rhein-Main air force base in late 1992 before this fellow had left. He did leave in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what was the response of Major Indic when you said that to him, and as closely to his words as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me how I knew about this. He was curious to know where I had learned this expression. And then he said yes. He said, "That's a form of punishment."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he -- or did you, rather, raise that in connection with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Major Indic make any comment as to the use of that technique in the context of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that they -- basically what he told me about his gunners was they were at will to hit the city when they wanted to, but in this particular case he didn't make any indication that he authorised such an action, but he was well aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he referred to his gunners, but which gunners were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gunners of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of which corps? Did you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't specifically state that. I did meet one of the men in Pale, at a coffee shop, coffee bar there, who indicated to me that he was a gunner, so I brought the subject up with him through my translator. And he laughed and said, "Oh, yes. I'm an expert at this." And then he proceeded to explain to me how he set the gun at a range of .2 degrees and fired upwards once they established the first round, and then the shells would go straight up a line and then they would move the gun and fire five shots at calibrated degrees across the city. He said they would average 8 to 10 shots up and 5 across. I was very surprised at how specific he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make any other comments in relation to that as to the usage of that technique?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fellow was particularly vehement towards Muslims. He made other comments, but I'm not -- I don't recall the actual remarks at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you meet the man at Pale, that gunner? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be in mid-1993, but it was later than the incident when I was talking to Indic. It was after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just confirm for us what was the elevation of the gun he referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elevation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Something about the degrees upwards that he --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. He said he would raise it .2 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: And fire one round and when they would mark the round off where they could it was hit when their spotter would report back where it hit, they would just raise the gun degree by degree, whatever it was, and fire 8 to 10 rounds and then they would recalibrate and fire right to left or left to right across the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm just wondering, I hope I'm not repeating myself, but do you recall any specific comment by Major Indic as to the use of that technique in Sarajevo? Do you recall him saying anything about -- further about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just that this was a form of punishment, but he didn't go into any great details about it. There was another comment, but I just can't recall what that was. He seemed a little bit surprised that I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he referred to it as a form of punishment. Did you ask him for any circumstances or description as to why they would in fact use that form of "punishment" in their action around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in that particular incident. Not in that particular context, in that particular discussion. I had already learned from the gentleman in Rhein-Main that had left Sarajevo, Republika Srpska, what it was about. It was in retaliation for an outgoing shell or a Serb soldier that had been wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you in fact raise that issue with Indic and invite any comment on that, the things you had learned from the man in Rhein-Main about why it was used? Did you raise it in any way, any further way with him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in any further context, not to my knowledge. I can't remember any -- it never came up again after that one time; I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during that time, did you have any -- sorry. Of all the incidents of your encounters with Indic that I've asked you about so far, did all of these take place within the period from, say, the end of 1992 to the middle August 1994? Are they within that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
